flaw.ctx: You asked for a 5-minute event counter.
flaw.answer: `_stamp[i] >= now - _w` includes the second exactly `window` seconds ago — a 301-second window. An event at t=0 is still counted at t=300.
flaw.fix: `> now - _w` (WindowCounter). Test exactly at the boundary, not one past it.

qa.a: Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).

qa.q: What does a bounded Channel do when full?
qa.a: Depends on `FullMode`. `Wait`: `WriteAsync` waits, `TryWrite` returns false. `DropWrite/DropNewest/DropOldest`: drops and `TryWrite` returns **true** (R14).

qa.q: When Interlocked instead of a lock?
qa.a: A single-word update with no invariant tying it to other fields — counters. Two fields that must agree need a lock.
SemaphoreSlim can be awaited (`WaitAsync`) and counts beyond 1; it is not re-entrant and must be released in a `finally`.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Count events in the last five minutes, at high rates, from many threads.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- `Record(nowSecs)`, `Count(nowSecs)`
- Memory bounded regardless of event rate
- Thread-safe

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: You do not need every event's timestamp — you need counts per second. A ring of 300 one-second buckets, each tagged with the second it holds, is O(window) memory whatever the rate. A stale bucket is detected by its tag and reset on reuse.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: Two arrays (stamp, count) indexed by `second % window`; one lock.

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Record: slot = now % W; if stamp[slot] ≠ now, reset it; count[slot] += n.
- Count: sum slots whose stamp is in (now − W, now].

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Type | Why |
|---|---|
| long[] stamp, int[] count | The ring; the stamp detects stale slots |
| lock | A Record is check-tag-then-increment — two steps, one invariant |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
- Record: slot = now % W; if stamp[slot] ≠ now, reset it; count[slot] += n.
- Count: sum slots whose stamp is in (now − W, now].

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md: Record O(1); Count O(W). Make Count O(1) with a running total adjusted as slots are recycled.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
- Events at 1, 1, 299, 300 → 4 at t=300; 2 at t=301 (second 1 left).
- A slot reused 600 s later is reset, not added to.
- 8 threads × 10,000 records → exactly 80,000.

learn.title: 10 · Tests
learn.md:
**S1 — Hits in the last five minutes**

- all four inside the window at 300
- second 1 leaves at 301
- a reused slot is reset
- exactly 300 s old is outside
- a million events

**S2 — Many threads record at once**

- no lost increments
- concurrent reads never go backwards
- all 80,000 counted

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Specify the structure ("ring of per-second buckets with a stamp array") — otherwise the assistant reaches for a queue of timestamps.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe a ring of per-second buckets, each tagged with the second it holds, gives O(window) memory whatever the event rate, and a stale tag tells me to reset a reused slot. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call Record and Count concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: Record and Count must be safe under concurrent callers with no lost increments. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- A `Queue<long>` of timestamps — O(events) memory.
- Not resetting a reused slot.
- `Interlocked` on count alone while the stamp reset is unprotected.

**Verification exercise:** Off-by-one — `_stamp[i] >= now - _w` includes the second exactly `window` seconds ago — a 301-second window. An event at t=0 is still counted at t=300.

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
Without the lock, two threads can both see a stale tag and both reset — losing one increment — or interleave reset and increment. Check-tag-then-act is the race.

**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Record from many threads.* — Stamp check-and-reset is the race → lock

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *Per user, ten million users.* — Sketches; coarser buckets

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
- This is the core of a rate limiter; say so if the conversation drifts there.

**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *Across machines.* — Local counters, periodic aggregation

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
- *Implement.* — Ring of buckets.
- *Thread-safe.* — One lock; or per-thread striped counters summed on read.
- *O(1) reads.* — Running total.
- *Per user, millions of users.* — Memory now matters: coarser buckets, or approximate (count-min sketch).
- *Across machines.* — Local counters, periodic aggregation; accept staleness.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Window edge — is an event exactly W seconds old counted?* — No: (now − W, now]

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Read cost?* — O(W); O(1) with a running total

stages.name: Hits in the last five minutes
stages.yours: Boundary first: an event at t counts while **now − t < window** (exactly 300 s old is **outside**). Structure: a ring of W per-second slots; slot = `t % W`; each slot remembers **which second** it holds, so a reused slot is reset.
bad: Count hits in the last 5 minutes.
A `Queue<long>` of timestamps — memory grows with traffic (a million events, a million entries) — with `>=` at the boundary.
No memory bound, so it stores every event
Boundary unstated, so it is guessed — usually wrong
good: Implement WindowCounter below: a ring of windowSecs slots, slot = now % windowSecs; each slot stores the second it holds and a count, and is reset when a new second lands on it. Count(now) sums the slots where now - second < windowSecs — an event exactly windowSecs old is OUTSIDE. Memory O(windowSecs), independent of traffic. No queue of timestamps. Keep my fields. State your assumptions about the boundary first. Show only Record and Count.
stages.reply: Typical defect (verified planted flaw R13): **`>= now - window`** — a 301-second window. An event at t=0 still counts at t=300.
validate: A reused slot is reset before counting
stages.say: "An event exactly five minutes old is out — I asked, and my boundary test pins it."
stages.require: Implement `Record` and `Count`. Memory must not grow with the number of events.
stages.say_iv: Count requests in the last five minutes, at ten thousand a second. Memory matters.

stages.name: Many threads record at once
stages.yours: Choose and say it: **one lock** around Record and Count is simplest and correct; `Interlocked` on the count alone is not enough, because the **slot reset** and the increment must be atomic together.
stages.ai: **AI writes the stress test** — with an exact expected total.
bad: `Interlocked.Increment` on the count, the slot reset left unprotected — a reset can wipe a concurrent increment.
The invariant (reset + increment together) is not named
Looks lock-free and fast, loses counts
good: Make Record and Count thread-safe with one lock — the slot reset and the increment must happen together. Then a stress test: 8 threads × 10,000 Record(1000); Count(1000) must be exactly 80,000; and a reader looping Count while 4 writers run must never see the total go down. Keep my fields and signatures. Explain why Interlocked alone is not enough. Show only the changed methods and the test.
stages.reply: Typical defect: the test asserts "about 80,000" or only "no exception" — it would pass with lost updates.
validate: Say the cost: one lock; striping per slot is the next step
stages.fix: If the test is approximate: **follow-up** — "Assert exactly 80,000."
stages.say: "The reset and the increment have to be atomic together, so a lock — Interlocked alone would lose counts at a second boundary."
stages.require: `Record` and `Count` must be safe under concurrent callers with no lost increments.
